t: For operation of trust programs for Indians by direct expenditure, contracts, cooperative agreements, compacts, and grants, $82,628,000, to remain available until expended: Provided, That funds for trust management improvements may be transferred, as needed, to the Bureau of Indian Affairs “Operation of Indian Programs” account and to the Departmental Management “Salaries and Expenses” account: Provided further, That funds made available to Tribes and Tribal organizations through contracts or grants obligated during fiscal year 2001, as authorized by the Indian Self-Determination Act of 1975 (25 U.S.C. 450 et seq.), shall remain available until expended by the contractor or grantee: Provided further, That notwithstanding any other provision of law, the statute of limitations shall not commence to run on any claim, including any claim in litigation pending on the date of the enactment of this Act, concerning losses to or mismanagement of trust funds, until the affected tribe or individual Indian has been furnished with an accounting of such funds from which the beneficiary can determine whether there has been a loss: Provided further, That notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Secretary shall not be required to provide a quarterly statement of performance for any Indian trust account that has not had activity for at least 18 months and has a balance of $1.00 or less: Provided further, That the Secretary shall issue an annual account statement and maintain a record of any such accounts and shall permit the balance in each such account to be withdrawn upon the express written request of the account holder.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the tolling proviso involves tribes and individual Indians suing the government over trust fund mismanagement. But it only adjusts when the limitations period begins for existing claims and does not grant a new right to sue or object to a federal decision, which the definition treats as a trap. The rest of the section is an appropriation, with contracts and grants to tribes, account statements and withdrawals on request, none of which is consultation with outside parties before a federal decision.
fable.s: the statute of limitations shall not commence to run on any claim, including any claim in litigation pending on the date of the enactment of this Act, concerning losses to or mismanagement of trust funds

opus.w: This is an appropriations provision covering how funds are made available, transfers between accounts, and rules for account statements. The tribal claims language only sets when the statute of limitations starts to run on existing claims. The DEFINITION treats this as a trap, because it describes litigation timing rather than granting a new right to challenge a federal decision. The contracts and grants to tribes are funding arrangements, not consultation before a federal decision, so no outside party takes part in federal decision-making here.
opus.s: the statute of limitations shall not commence to run on any claim, including any claim in litigation pending on the date of the enactment of this Act, concerning losses to or mismanagement of trust funds, until the affected tribe or individual Indian has been furnished with an accounting of such funds
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading:** The provision on the statute of limitations for claims by tribes and individual Indians over mismanaged trust funds could look like it gives outside parties the right to sue. The contracts, compacts and grants with tribes could also look like tribal involvement in federal decisions. Neither holds up. The DEFINITION lists statute-of-limitations rules as a trap, because describing when a suit can be filed is not the same as creating a right to sue. Contracts and grants are funding arrangements, not consultation. Letting account holders withdraw their balances on request is an account service, not input into a federal decision.

2. **Label:**

qwen_chat.w: This section primarily deals with appropriations and procedural rules for trust fund management and litigation. The mention of furnishing an accounting to tribes is a unilateral administrative duty to enable the calculation of a statute of limitations, not a consultation or coordination process before a federal decision. The definition explicitly excludes statute-of-limitations periods and applications for benefits/grants. There is no requirement for the government to consult with outsiders before making a decision.
qwen_chat.s: Provided further, That notwithstanding any other provision of law, the statute of limitations shall not commence to run on any claim, including any claim in litigation pending on the date of the enactment of this Act, concerning losses to or mismanagement of trust funds, until the affected tribe or individual Indian has been furnished with an accounting of such funds from which the beneficiary can determine whether there has been a loss
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the provision regarding the statute of limitations for trust fund claims implies participation because it mentions "affected tribe or individual Indian" and "accounting." However, this is a procedural rule regarding litigation timelines and record-keeping, not a requirement for the government to consult with outsiders before making a decision. The definition explicitly excludes "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits" and "applications for benefits." The accounting is a unilateral duty of the Secretary, not a collaborative process.
